groups.title: Seed-based restoration of eelgrass: the Solberg procedure

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Seagrass meadows rarely attract the attention that coral reefs or rainforests do, yet they are among the most productive habitats on Earth. Although they occupy less than 0.2 per cent of the ocean floor, they are estimated to bury about 10 per cent of the carbon that is stored in marine sediments each year. They also stabilise the seabed, filter particles from the water, and provide shelter for juvenile fish, including several species of commercial importance. Their dense leaves slow the movement of water, which allows fine particles to settle and helps to protect shorelines from erosion during storms. Despite this, about 30 per cent of the world's seagrass area is thought to have disappeared since the late nineteenth century, and in many regions the losses are continuing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The causes of decline are well documented. Fertilisers washed from farmland feed blooms of algae, which block the sunlight that seagrass needs to photosynthesise. Dredging for ports and the scarring caused by anchors and propellers remove plants directly, while warming seas have encouraged a wasting disease that can strip a meadow within weeks. For many years, restoration meant simply moving mature plants from healthy meadows to damaged sites. The method was labour-intensive, it damaged the donor meadows, and in most trials fewer than one in ten transplanted shoots survived the first winter storms. Conservationists began to ask whether the plants' own reproductive cycle might offer a better route.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The alternative took shape in the early 2000s in Kessing Bay, a shallow inlet on the Baltic coast, where a team led by Dr Ingrid Solberg of the University of Bergen had observed that eelgrass flowers in early summer and produces thousands of seeds on every shoot. Her team's procedure, now widely copied, begins in June, when volunteers collect flowering shoots by hand from healthy meadows, taking only a small fraction of the plants in any one place. The shoots are carried ashore and held in tanks of aerated seawater, where the seeds ripen and are gradually released over several weeks. Once the seeds have dropped, staff pass the water through fine sieves to separate them from fragments of leaf. The seeds are then stored in cold tanks until October, because they will not germinate until the water temperature falls. Finally, they are sown from small boats, either scattered by hand or injected into the sediment through tubes.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Sowing alone proved disappointing. In Solberg's early trials only about 3 per cent of seeds grew into seedlings, because crabs ate many seeds and strong currents buried or washed away others. Dr Tomas Ferreira of the University of Lisbon, working in a tidal lagoon in southern Portugal, proposed packing seeds into small hessian bags that are pegged to the seabed. The bags protect the seeds from predators and hold them in place until roots have formed; the hessian itself rots away within a few months. In a three-year trial, establishment rose to 17 per cent, although Ferreira cautions that the bags are expensive to make and to lay, and may not be suitable for large exposed areas.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A second problem concerns genetic diversity. Seeds are often gathered from a handful of convenient meadows, so restored beds may consist of closely related plants. Dr Aiko Tanabe of Hokkaido University monitored restored meadows in northern Japan through a marine heatwave in 2018. Those grown from a single source lost nearly half their shoots, whereas those sown with a mixture of seeds from at least five sites lost about one fifth. Tanabe argues that diversity works like insurance: a varied population is more likely to contain some plants able to tolerate unusual conditions. Her recommendations have since been incorporated into several national restoration guidelines, and a number of seed banks now record the origin of every batch they supply so that managers can combine material from distant sites with confidence.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Where restoration has succeeded, the ecological returns have been rapid. Within five years of sowing, restored beds in Kessing Bay held densities of juvenile fish comparable to those of natural meadows, and the sediment beneath them had begun to accumulate carbon. Even so, most researchers agree that planting cannot compensate for continuing pollution. A restored meadow in water still clouded by fertiliser runoff will fail, however carefully it was sown. Solberg therefore regards seed-based restoration as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, tighter controls on farming and coastal development. Some governments are considering whether the carbon stored by new meadows could be sold as credits to fund such work, but the accounting methods remain unsettled. Others worry that such schemes might encourage developers to damage existing meadows on the assumption that new ones can easily be planted elsewhere.
